If you're wondering...

Why aren't you actually supposed to dig?

It seems so obvious: you plunge the spade into the ground, turn the sod over, and you have a fresh, airy soil ready for a new season. Generations of gardeners have done it this way. And yet digging is one of the most damaging things you can do to your soil.

The reason lies below the surface — literally. Healthy soil isn't a dead medium. It's a living network of fungi, bacteria, worms, and microscopic organisms organized into fine layers. Each layer has its own inhabitants, its own function, its own balance. When you dig, you completely turn that system upside down. The layer that belonged on top ends up on the bottom. The organisms that need light are suddenly in the dark. The fungal threads that took years to weave themselves together are shredded in a single motion.

Digging doesn't even solve, in the short term, the problem it claims to solve. Yes, the soil feels looser. But that looseness is temporary. After the first rain, the soil compacts again — often more than before digging, because the soil structure that kept it open has been destroyed. So you create a problem you have to solve all over again every year, with the spade.

Nature doesn't dig. In a forest, the soil is never turned over, and yet it's richer, looser, and more fertile than any vegetable garden. That's because the soil organizes itself: leaves fall, decompose, become humus. Worms dig tunnels that let water through. Roots break up hard layers. The system works — if you let it.

Not digging isn't laziness. It's trust in a system millions of years older than the spade.
